title: AI Coding Assistants Compared: How to Pick One
description:
A practical comparison framework for choosing an AI coding assistant based on how you actually work, not just feature lists.

#AICoding #DevTools #Programming

scenes.narration: There are a dozen AI coding assistants now, and they're not all built for the same kind of work. Here's how to actually choose.

First question: are you writing new code or maintaining an existing large codebase? Some assistants are tuned for fast autocomplete in a small file, great for prototyping, while others are built to hold an entire project's context and reason across multiple files at once, which matters a lot more once your codebase gets big.
If you work mostly inside one editor, an assistant that lives directly in that editor beats one you have to alt-tab to.

Second question: do you want it to just suggest, or actually make changes across files for you? Autocomplete-style tools are lower risk and easier to review line by line. Agentic tools that edit multiple files save more time but need you to actually read the diff before trusting it, especially early on while you're learning where it tends to go wrong.
Also check how it handles your existing code style. A good assistant should match your formatting, not fight it.

Third question: cost and limits. Free tiers are usually generous enough for side projects and learning, but heavy daily professional use often needs a paid tier eventually. Test the free tier on a real task first, not a toy example, before deciding if it's worth paying for.
There's no single best assistant, there's the one that fits how you already work. Try two on the same real task and see which one actually saves you time, not which one has the longer feature list.
Which one are you using? Drop it in the comments, and subscribe for more dev-focused AI breakdowns.
